Area.evidence_source: The main findings of this study are that suicidal thoughts following sexual violence are based on an experienced 'strong self-destruction force' that involves almost unbearable suffering which is still unexpressed but primarily focused on avoiding frequent thoughts about the violence and finding peace. The strong self-destruction force resulted in participants' risk behaviour, such as driving too fast without seatbelts, high drinking and consumption of other drugs to kill the emotional pain, as well as total indifference to their own health and life. Discussions in society about sexual violence could increase their suicidal ideation. Much stress also resulted in more suicidal ideation. They were so used to thinking of death that it became part of everyday life. Destructive thoughts, lack of selfesteem and loneliness characterised their life and hopelessness were common. They felt they were bad and worthless human beings and talked about disconnection of body and mind. Participants reported unexplained physical pain and other health problems they associated with the violence. Common societal norms about male sexual violence survivors had a major negative impact on all participants. The most common was the masculine image of the strong silent man who should not express any emotional pain which had a very negative effect on their emotional life and involved a certain emotional silencing. A common myth the men were dealing with was that men cannot be raped by a woman which prevented their disclosure about such violence. They also reported the fear that they would themselves become perpetrators, or be judged as such, as they felt that myth was strong in society. Disclosing the violence proved extremely difficult for them, but they experienced a high level of positive energy after disclosure. The reaction of others mattered, and trauma-specific support was very important to them.
